analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug company monopolies with government prizes so all makers can compete on price.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: Senator Sanders introduced it alone with no cosponsors, a Senate subcommittee held one hearing in May 2012, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip drug and biologic makers of their exclusive rights to sell patented medicines, effective October 2012. Instead of earning monopoly profits by charging high prices for 10-plus years, innovators would be paid cash prizes from a federal fund based on how much a new medicine actually helps patients. Generic and competing manufacturers could make any drug the day it clears approval, driving prices toward production cost. The fund would spend about 0.55 percent of U.S. GDP — over $80 billion in 2011 — raised through federal appropriations and an annual fee on health insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and insurers who buy medicines: prices would fall to competitive levels immediately upon approval because any manufacturer could make the drug. A small portion of the prize fund is reserved for neglected tropical diseases, rare orphan diseases, and global infectious disease work — areas that monopoly pricing currently underserves because poor patients cannot pay high prices. Open-source researchers who share data freely would also earn a share of the prizes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends every legal basis for exclusive drug marketing — patents, Hatch-Waxman exclusivity, orphan-drug exclusivity, pediatric extensions, and the 30-month stay — so any company could manufacture and sell any approved medicine in competition [S3][S2].

Innovators would be paid from a prize fund instead, with rewards judged by number of patients helped and how much the drug improves on existing treatments, rather than by sales volume at monopoly prices [S3][S2].

At least 18 percent of the fund is reserved as minimums for global neglected diseases (4%), orphan diseases (10%), and global infectious diseases and other priorities including AIDS and bioterrorism countermeasures (4%) [S3].
At least 5 percent of prize payments would go to 'open source dividend' prizes for researchers and communities that share knowledge, data, and technology royalty-free [S3].
The Government Accountability Office would audit the prize board every year to check whether it is actually getting new medicines to market cost-effectively [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an appropriation of 0.55 percent of GDP each year (the bill's own figures put that above $80 billion in 2011), and health insurers, which would pay an annual fee scaled to their premium volume, exempting small insurers with under $25 million in premiums [S3].

drawbacks.text: The program is very large: an annual appropriation of 0.55 percent of GDP — over $80 billion per year by the bill's own estimate — would be one of the biggest new federal programs, raised partly by a fee on health insurers that could be passed into premiums [S3].

Prizes replace a price signal with a government board's judgment. If the 13-member Board of Trustees systematically underpaid or misjudged a drug's value, investment in that therapy area could fall, with no market mechanism to correct it until the annual GAO audit [S3].

Ending all exclusive rights from October 1, 2012 applies retroactively to products already on the market, so companies that priced in expectation of decades of exclusivity would absorb a sudden loss of future monopoly revenue during the transition [S3].

Prize decisions would depend heavily on who sits on the Board and its advisory committees; the bill requires transparency and conflict-of-interest rules but gives the Board wide discretion over award criteria [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: patients would pay near-cost prices for every medicine, in exchange for a large, permanent federal outlay and a shift from market pricing to government-judged rewards. If the prize board were well-run, the gains to patients dwarf the cost, since the country currently pays monopoly prices for the same innovation. But the design is an untested, sweeping experiment in one bill — no phase-in of pricing freedom, no country has done this at this scale — and its success would rest entirely on the judgment of the prize board. The bill's failure was not for lack of a coherent idea; it never received serious consideration.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never took it up; a subcommittee held a single hearing in May 2012, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill alone on May 26, 2011; no senator signed on as a cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never ordered a vote on it [S5].
The committee's Subcommittee on Primary Health and Aging held a hearing with a printed record (S.Hrg. 112-570) on May 15, 2012 — the only committee action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill never reached the Senate floor and died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the exclusive marketing rights the bill would have ended, and health insurers never had to pay the new annual fee. Patients continued to pay monopoly prices for patented medicines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept their monopolies

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out or scheduled a markup; the full committee took no action in two Congress-years.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no party split is recorded; the bill's only supporter was an independent senator and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would erase their exclusive right to sell patented drugs — the source of industry revenue priced well above manufacturing cost — and replace it with capped prize payments of at most 10 years per product and 5% of the fund per product. Their interest in keeping the exclusivity system runs directly against cheaper medicines for patients.

With no exclusivity, generic makers could produce every newly approved drug immediately instead of waiting years for patents and exclusivity periods to lapse, giving them a vastly larger market. Their gain is the same as the public's gain: competition at low prices.

Insurers above the small-employer threshold would pay an annual fee scaled to premiums to fund the prizes, but they are also among the largest buyers of medicines and would benefit from drug prices falling toward production cost. The net effect depends on whether savings on drugs exceed the new fee.
